blogs.title: The Federal Circuit Reaffirms De Novo Review When Denying Judgment as a Matter of Law
blogs.description: This post analyses how the Ninth‑Circuit’s reversal in "Finesse Wireless v. AT&T" demonstrates that a district court’s denial of a JMOL must be reviewed de novo under Fifth‑Circuit precedent such as *Wi‑LAN*. It explains the evidence threshold – that only overwhelmingly strong proof beyond any reasoned jury conclusion will survive reverse – discusses the new emphasis on thorough claim‑construction scrutiny when limited evidence is presented, and outlines practical implications for litigants who rely heavily on expert testimony in complex telecom patent wars.

blogs.title: Marriage Between Claims and Amendments: What ‘Three Signals’ Add Up To
blogs.description: Turning attention to patent drafting doctrine, this essay looks at how Finesse’s amendment tightening "three signals S1,S2,S3" failed to disavow two‑signal usage because it was not "clear and unambiguous" per *Cont’l Circuits v. Intel*. By comparing this case with earlier objections such as *Filipovic*, we uncover what constitutes a true scope‑reduction during prosecution history edits—a lesson especially vital when tailoring interference‑mitigation tech claims that may rest upon subtle numeric distinctions.

blogs.title: When Expert Statements Don't Sync With Hardware – Lessons from Dr. Wells
blogs.description: The decision pivots heavily on Senior Judge Moore’s criticism that Dr Wells’s testimony was contradictory about whether sampled PIM paths were "interference generating signals" or merely modeled outputs fed through an FPGA. Here we dissect how appellate panels test experts’ logical coherence against actual block‑diagram data, showing why lawyers must guard against ambiguous affiliations between diagram names like "DL(TX)” & “modeled PIM” versus concrete signal paths x1/x2 during pre‑trial prep.

blogs.title: Why $166 Million Vanishes Once Infringement Is Doubtful
blogs.description: This post explores the intertwined fate of verdicts and damages once nonenforcement findings prevail. By vacating nearly $166m after finding no substantial evidence supporting infringement claims, the federal court underscores that cash awards hinge restingly squarely on juror conclusions—not merely faculty-level technology predictions—while also touching upon policy themes around punitive escalation versus real world unit conversions amid uncertain technical assertions.
